A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAUQ research despite the changed title. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are accessible and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments across four LLMs, attention-pattern analyses, ablations, supervised-method comparisons, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments with additional model configurations, method variants, head-selection analyses, and manually categorized generation errors.

M1.justification: The core head selection, recurrence, and aggregation remain intact. Section 4 generalizes the token-confidence input to permit an entropy-based signal, adopted for instruction-tuned models. Appendix C.5 also introduces a variant replacing attention weights with Layer Integrated Gradients. These are localized procedural extensions.

E1.justification: The same seven QA datasets, three summarization datasets, and French-English and German-English translation benchmarks remain covered. The additional model experiments and qualitative examples use this existing coverage; they do not establish new tasks, domains, or language pairs.

E2.justification: v3 adds Mean Token Entropy as an evaluated comparator in the instruction-tuned comparison, Table 16. The original four-model comparison retains its 15 baselines, including Simple Focus, and the corresponding supervised comparisons retain all seven methods.

E3.justification: v3 adds 360M, 1B, and 70B models plus two instruction-tuned models. The stated summarization alpha changes from 0 to 0.2 for base models, while instruction-tuned experiments use 0.9. The summarization ROC-AUC threshold changes from 0.3 to 0.5. New evaluation designs include head selection using 100 held-out instances per task and inspection of 20 highest- and 20 lowest-uncertainty examples.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained aggregation and recurrence ablations, v3 tests relative attention drops, probability versus entropy signals, layer subsets, head-selection stability, fixed versus dynamic heads, and substitution with attribution scores. Appendices E and F add summarization/translation case studies and an error analysis distinguishing factual and reasoning errors. These substantially expand examination of the method's components and failure behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark performance. The runtime values with plus/minus reporting are retained unchanged from v2 Table 4 in v3 Table 3. Newly reported frequencies and error percentages are additional results, not new uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Summarization results are extensively replaced: for example, Qwen RAUQ's summarization PRR in Table 1 changes from 0.415 to 0.213, below Perplexity's new 0.254. These accompany revised settings and do not establish a same-setting decline. Supervised-comparison and ablation values also change, while new model, attribution, and error-analysis tables add substantial results. Table 25 reports errors in 95% of the highest-uncertainty sample and 50% of the lowest-uncertainty sample.

T1.justification: v3 corrects the cross-head average in Section 3 by including 1/H and adds mathematical definitions for entropy-based confidence and attention-normalization variants. Section 4 also introduces an eigenvalue/log-determinant argument. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs; much of the new 'theoretical grounding' is conceptual interpretation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: an unsupervised, single-pass attention-based uncertainty method with state-of-the-art performance and less than 1% overhead. Updating the evaluation from four to nine LLMs expands supporting evidence without redefining that core contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds mechanism explanations connecting attention to local continuity, pretraining, and reliance on global priors. It interprets the new analyses as supporting stable head selection, entropy-based confidence for instruction-tuned models, and possible extension beyond standard attention. Section 5.2 acknowledges summarization exceptions to the earlier uniformly best results, while the error discussion identifies common misbeliefs among low-uncertainty errors.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository reference and specifies the previously vague middle-layer choice as the middle third, including layers 10–22 for Llama-3.1 8B. It additionally documents attention-format normalization, Simple Focus components, attribution-score construction, and use of the input document as the summarization AlignScore reference. These are useful disclosures; the PDFs do not establish that every newly described implementation detail changed.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting head specialization, integrated gradients, additional model families, and uncertainty estimation, including Elhelo and Geva, Sundararajan et al., and Aichberger et al. It expands its connection to Sriramanan et al.'s attention analysis while retaining the existing research positioning. The updated TAD publication is the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: The abstract and several related-work and method paragraphs are rewritten, and the method exposition is reorganized around three motivating ideas. Dataset, baseline, and metric descriptions move into Appendix A; the appendices are reorganized; the impact statement moves before the references; and the conclusion gains future work. The title and author-affiliation presentation also change.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main-text layout, merges v2 Figures 3 and 4 into Figure 3, and replaces Figure 2's layer-22 heatmaps with layer-23 heatmaps. The runtime table moves into the main text. Numerous new ablation, model-comparison, and error-analysis tables and six summarization/translation attention maps substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 improves reproducibility and scrutiny through explicit layer-selection details, a code reference, broader model testing, head-selection controls, and an informative failure analysis absent from v2. It also qualifies the summarization advantage. However, new reporting problems temper these benefits: Appendix C.1 calls RAUQ second for 70B QA although Table 15 places several baselines above it, and Section 4 incorrectly equates an eigenvalue sum with a log determinant. The added evidence and transparency support a limited net quality improvement.
